AssemLM: Spatial Reasoning Multimodal Large Language Models for Robotic Assembly

Zhi Jing    Jinbin Qiao Affiliation: Tianjin University    Ouyang Lu Affiliation: Northwestern Polytechnical University    Jicong Ao    Shuang Qiu Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong*Corresponding author    Yu-Gang Jiang    Chenjia Bai Affiliation: Fudan University Affiliation: Institute of Artificial Intelligence (TeleAI), China Telecom Affiliation: Equally leading organizationshttps://assemlmhome.github.io/
Abstract

Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability for embodied intelligence, especially for fine-grained manipulation tasks such as robotic assembly. While recent vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit preliminary spatial awareness, they largely rely on coarse 2D perception and lack the ability to perform accurate reasoning over 3D geometry, which is crucial for precise assembly operations. To address this limitation, we propose AssemLM, a spatial multimodal large language model tailored for robotic assembly. AssemLM integrates assembly manuals, point clouds, and textual instructions to reason about and predict task-critical 6D assembly poses, enabling explicit geometric understanding throughout the assembly process. To effectively bridge raw 3D perception and high-level reasoning, we adopt a specialized point cloud encoder to capture fine-grained geometric and rotational features, which are then integrated into the multimodal language model to support accurate 3D spatial reasoning for assembly tasks. In addition, we construct AssemBench, a large-scale dataset and benchmark for assembly-oriented spatial reasoning, comprising over 900K multimodal samples with precise 6D pose annotations. AssemBench extends spatial reasoning evaluation beyond 2D and grounding tasks into full 3D geometric inference, filling a critical gap in existing embodied AI benchmarks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AssemLM  achieves state-of-the-art performance in 6D pose reasoning across diverse assembly scenarios. Furthermore, real-robot evaluations show that our model can support fine-grained and multi-step assembly execution in real-world settings, demonstrating its potential for robotic assembly applications.

I Introduction

From assembling furniture [4, 19, 24, 41, 42] to repairing appliances [17, 28] and reconstructing fragmented objects [21, 34, 36, 47], assembly processes are ubiquitous in daily life. Enabling robots to assist in such tasks can significantly reduce human effort and improve accessibility for non-expert users. These tasks are fundamentally important yet highly challenging for embodied intelligence, as they require fine-grained geometric reasoning over task-critical 6D poses at each step. Achieving this necessitates not only accurate pose prediction, but also the ability to jointly interpret multimodal inputs, including language instructions, point clouds, and visual observations, as well as to generalize across diverse object categories and instance-level variations.

Despite recent progress, achieving generalization across diverse object categories and robust multimodal understanding remains challenging. On the one hand, assembly processes are inherently compositional, involving diverse object categories and instance-level geometric variations. Recent works [33, 36, 42, 47, 49] demonstrate promising capabilities in assembly pose prediction, but are largely restricted to specific object categories and primarily rely on single-modal inputs such as point clouds, limiting their generalization across diverse categories. On the other hand, complete assembly inference requires jointly interpreting language instructions, visual cues, and geometric observations to understand the current state. Recent spatial reasoning models such as RoboBrain [22, 40] and RoboRefer [51] extend image–language models with depth information, enabling basic spatial understanding. However, they remain insufficient for predicting precise task-critical 6D poses required in assembly tasks. Moreover, large-scale multimodal datasets featuring diverse object categories and precise part poses are essential to train and evaluate models for assembly-oriented spatial reasoning. Existing datasets [4, 35, 38] offer useful samples but are limited in scale and lack comprehensive modality coverage, thus failing to effectively support unified multimodal learning for large-scale model training.

To address these challenges, we present AssemLM, a spatial multimodal large language model for robotic assembly reasoning. AssemLM employs a specialized point cloud encoder to extract fine-grained geometric and equivariant rotational features, addressing the limitations of coarse 2D perception. These 3D representations are integrated into a multimodal transformer backbone that jointly processes manuals, text, and 3D geometries, enabling explicit geometric reasoning and precise 6D pose prediction.

To address the critical lack of large-scale multimodal data for robotic assembly, we introduce AssemBench, a comprehensive benchmark containing over 900K multimodal samples derived from 150K distinct assembly steps, spanning diverse object categories including furniture, daily objects, and fragments. We also develop an automated data generation pipeline that converts raw mesh assets and large-scale web-collected visual resources into high-fidelity point clouds, visual manuals, and aligned linguistic instructions. This provides large-scale, high-precision supervision for 6D pose grounding in assembly tasks, enabling models to learn from a diverse range of part geometries and spatial configurations.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose AssemLM, a spatial multimodal large language model designed for robotic assembly that enables accurate prediction of task-critical 6D assembly poses, effectively bridging raw 3D perception and high-level reasoning for robotic assembly.

  • •

    We introduce AssemBench, a large-scale multimodal benchmark for assembly-oriented spatial reasoning that jointly includes manuals, point clouds, and textual instructions, comprising over 900K samples with precise 6D pose annotations across diverse assembly categories.

  • •

    We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across diverse object categories, highlighting strong generalization capabilities, and further show the model’s potential for real-world robotic assembly through real-robot evaluations.

II Related Work

II-A Spatial Reasoning with Large Multimodal Models

Perceiving and reasoning about spatial information is fundamental for embodied foundation models in real-world manipulation. Prior work on spatial reasoning broadly falls into two categories: 1) Semantic-level spatial reasoning focuses on qualitative relations such as relative position and orientation without explicit metric grounding. Representative methods include SpatialVLM [6] and SpatialRGPT [10], which enable coarse spatial understanding across image and point cloud modalities. 2) Numeric-level spatial reasoning aims to infer explicit quantitative attributes, including position, rotation, and depth. Approaches such as SpatialBot [5], RoboBrain [22, 40], and RoboRefer [51] incorporate metric grounding via RGB-D or multimodal perception.

Despite these advances, existing methods remain limited in rotation reasoning [48] and rely heavily on 2D pixel–depth representations [5, 18, 22, 26], which cannot fully capture the 3D geometric structure essential for accurate 6D pose estimation in assembly tasks. Our method addresses this by performing equivariant 3D spatial reasoning directly on point clouds, enabling precise and robust 6D pose prediction in complex assembly tasks.

II-B Assembly Datasets and Benchmarks

Robotic assembly datasets originate from object reassembly and part-based reconstruction in computer vision. Existing benchmarks can be grouped into four categories. 1) Everyday object assembly includes Assembly101 [35], which provides large-scale multi-view recordings of human toy-vehicle assembly with dense action and hand-pose annotations. 2) Furniture assembly is represented by IKEAASM [4], featuring multi-view videos with fine-grained action, segmentation, and pose labels. 3) Fragment reassembly focuses on reconstructing fractured objects, exemplified by BreakingBad [34], which offers over one million simulated broken parts. 4) Robotic assembly benchmarks typically target narrow tasks such as peg-in-hole or gear assembly, e.g., ReAssemble [38], with limited object diversity and scale.

Many recent works leverage vision-language models to generate IKEA-style manuals [27, 42, 45, 49], but remain largely confined to furniture assembly and primarily rely on image or point cloud modalities. In this work, we introduce AssemBench, a large-scale multimodal benchmark comprising over 900K samples and 150K+ assembly steps, enabling systematic research on multimodal robotic assembly at scale.

II-C 6D Assembly Pose Prediction for Robotic Manipulation

Accurate 6D pose prediction at each assembly step is crucial for successful assembly execution. Most existing methods rely on single modality point cloud inputs and emphasize SE(3) equivariant representations for geometric reasoning. Specifically, SE(3)-Transformer [16] introduces equivariant attention mechanisms for 3D roto-translation symmetry, while Vector Neurons [12] provides a general framework for SO(3)-equivariant learning by encoding features as 3D vectors instead of scalar activations. EPN [7] and 3D EGIF [9] further extend equivariant representations to point cloud analysis and implicit function modeling, respectively. Building upon this line of work, SE(3)-Assembly [47] and TwoByTwo [33] demonstrate the effectiveness of SE(3)-equivariant point cloud reasoning for assembly pose prediction. However, their reliance on point clouds alone limits multimodal integration, and their cross-category generalization is mainly limited to categories within a single broad domain, e.g., within fragments or within daily objects, rather than across diverse assembly domains. To address this, our approach integrates SE(3) equivariant geometric features into a multimodal large language model, enabling unified multi-category, multimodal 6D assembly pose prediction with strong generalization capabilities.

III Methods

III-A Problem Formulation

Consider an assembly object 𝒪\mathcal{O} composed of nn parts 𝒪={o0,…,on−1}\mathcal{O}=\{o_{0},\dots,o_{n-1}\} with n≥2n\geq 2, ordered according to the predefined assembly sequence. The assembly of the object 𝒪\mathcal{O} requires at least n−1n-1 sequential steps, 𝒮={s1,…,sn−1}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{n-1}\}, to incrementally assemble the object. At step sis_{i}, the previously assembled parts are treated as a single fixed entity, denoted by 𝒪ifixed={o0,…,oi−1}\mathcal{O}^{\text{fixed}}_{i}=\{o_{0},\dots,o_{i-1}\}, and the part to be assembled is defined as the moving part, 𝒪imoving={oi}\mathcal{O}^{\text{moving}}_{i}=\{o_{i}\}.

The model’s objective is to leverage multimodal inputs to predict a 6-DoF SE(3) pose, which represents the rigid transformation required to assemble 𝒪imoving\mathcal{O}^{\text{moving}}_{i} onto 𝒪ifixed\mathcal{O}^{\text{fixed}}_{i}. This is achieved by taking the following inputs: the point clouds 𝒫ifixed\mathcal{P}^{\text{fixed}}_{i} and 𝒫imoving\mathcal{P}^{\text{moving}}_{i} sampled from 𝒪ifixed\mathcal{O}^{\text{fixed}}_{i} and 𝒪imoving\mathcal{O}^{\text{moving}}_{i}, the manual images IibeforeI_{i}^{\text{before}} and IiafterI_{i}^{\text{after}}, which are rendered images depicting the assembled parts before and after step sis_{i}, and the assembly instruction lil_{i}.

III-B AssemLM: Multimodal Spatial Reasoning for Robotic Assembly

We introduce AssemLM, a 2B-parameter spatial multimodal large model based on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct [2], designed to predict precise 6D poses for sequential assembly steps. As illustrated in Fig. 2, we incorporate four key architectural innovations: explicit geometric equivariance in 3D perception, embedding-level multimodal fusion for enhanced spatial grounding, specialized assembly pose tokenizer, and an optimized supervised fine-tuning (SFT) pipeline.

Explicit Geometric Equivariance in 3D Perception. To empower the LLM backbone with robust spatial grounding against arbitrary rigid body transformations, we inject SE(3)-equivariant representations into the reasoning pipeline. Unlike conventional point encoders (e.g., PointNet [32]) that often discard pose information or rely on data augmentation, we employ a specialized Vector Neuron DGCNN [12, 47] to extract features that explicitly track both the orientation and position of assembly parts.

Formally, the encoder takes a point cloud P∈ℝN×3P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} as input and utilizes dual branches to extract SE(3)-equivariant features F=ℰequiv​(P)F=\mathcal{E}_{\text{equiv}}(P) and SE(3)-invariant features G=ℰinv​(P)G=\mathcal{E}_{\text{inv}}(P). For any rigid transformation T∈S​E​(3)T\in SE(3) composed of rotation RR and translation tt (i.e., T⁡(P)=R​P+tT(P)=RP+t), these features satisfy:

ℰequiv​(R​P+t)=R⋅ℰequiv​(P)+t,\mathcal{E}_{\text{equiv}}(RP+t)=R\cdot\mathcal{E}_{\text{equiv}}(P)+t, (1)
ℰinv​(R​P+t)=ℰinv​(P).\mathcal{E}_{\text{inv}}(RP+t)=\mathcal{E}_{\text{inv}}(P). (2)

This formulation ensures that FF faithfully preserves the object’s 6D pose in the feature space, while GG encodes pure geometric shape descriptors independent of spatial placement.

To ground the assembly alignment, we construct a geometric correlation CC by modulating the equivariant pose of the moving part (FmovingF_{\text{moving}}) with the invariant shape context of the fixed part (GfixedG_{\text{fixed}}):

C=Gfixed⋅Fmoving,C∈ℝf×3.C=G_{\text{fixed}}\cdot F_{\text{moving}},\quad C\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times 3}. (3)

Crucially, since GfixedG_{\text{fixed}} is invariant, the correlation CC retains the SE(3)-equivariance of the moving part. This enables the multimodal LLM to capture the spatial state of the moving component relative to the target geometry, facilitating precise 6D pose prediction.

Finally, to resolve cases where the fixed part itself is non-canonical, we incorporate FfixedF_{\text{fixed}} as complementary context. Both CC and FfixedF_{\text{fixed}} are projected into the LLM embedding space, providing a physics-grounded geometric prior for assembly planning.

Multimodal Fusion and Spatial Grounding. To align visual cues from assembly manuals with 3D geometric reasoning, we perform multimodal fusion directly at the embedding level, avoiding the overhead of complex cross-attention modules while enabling efficient integration. We employ a vision encoder based on SigLIP-2 [2, 13, 43] to extract dense visual representations, which are projected into the LLM latent space.

To preserve both high-level semantics and fine-grained spatial details, we incorporate a DeepStack mechanism [1, 2], which projects and injects intermediate features from multiple encoder layers into early transformer layers. This multi-scale approach ensures that the model maintains the high-fidelity contextual grounding required for precise manipulation.

The point cloud embeddings are injected into the sequence via modality-specific placeholders. By preserving the original visual token layout and utilizing M-ROPE (Multimodal Rotary Positional Embedding) [3] derived from the visual grid, we aim to preserve the LLM’s inherent visual-spatial reasoning capability when incorporating 3D inputs.

This unified embedding sequence enables the backbone to jointly reason over textual instructions, assembly manuals, and 3D geometries within a consistent spatial reference frame, significantly enhancing long-context stability for complex assembly planning.

Specialized Assembly Pose Tokenization. We cast assembly pose prediction as a language modeling task by extending the Qwen3-VL tokenizer with a dedicated pose vocabulary. Specifically, we introduce 201 discrete tokens {<assemble_pose_0>,…,<assemble_pose_200>}\{\texttt{<assemble\_pose\_0>},\dots,\texttt{<assemble\_pose\_200>}\} to represent coordinate values. To enable stable geometric learning, we represent each 6D assembly pose as a 9D pose vector, composed of 3D translation and a 6D continuous rotation representation [52]. This representation avoids the discontinuities inherent in Euler angles or quaternions, facilitating smoother optimization for the LLM backbone.

All nine dimensions are normalized to [−1,1][-1,1] and uniformly discretized into 201 bins. This uniform tokenization strategy offers several advantages: 1) Seamless Integration: It enables end-to-end autoregressive decoding without requiring auxiliary continuous regression heads or complex pretrained tokenizers. 2) Reduced Predictive Burden: By maintaining a fixed 9-token sequence length for any pose, it avoids the redundancy and variable-length instability of generic subword tokenizers (e.g., FastTokenizer [31]), thereby providing a more stable interface for high-precision grounding. 3) Initialization Stability: The embeddings for new action tokens are initialized using the mean of existing linguistic embeddings, ensuring training stability during the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase.

Optimized Supervised Fine-tuning Pipeline. We implement a two-stage training strategy to decouple geometric feature acquisition from multimodal reasoning, ensuring training stability for complex assembly tasks.

During the initial Geometry Warm-up phase, we pre-train the point cloud encoder alone on a targeted subset of AssemBench without linguistic supervision. Concretely, an MLP projector is attached to the encoder to directly predict the assembly pose, supervised by an L1 loss for translation and a Geodesic Distance loss for rotation. The projector is introduced solely for this warm-up stage and is discarded afterward; only the pre-trained encoder is retained in the subsequent multimodal training stage. This process encourages the encoder to ground its SE(3)-equivariant features in pure geometric structures before multimodal fusion.

In the subsequent Full Multimodal Alignment phase, we jointly optimize all modalities on the complete dataset. Crucially, we treat pose prediction as a standard language modeling objective by applying cross-entropy loss only to the 9-token pose span, while masking out other tokens. This alignment with the Next Token Prediction paradigm facilitates the seamless integration of AssemLM into broader embodied AI frameworks.

III-C AssemBench

Overview. AssemBench is a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for spatial reasoning in robotic assembly, integrating visual assembly manuals, 3D point clouds, and precise natural language assembly instructions (see Fig. 3). Its key features are: 1) Large Scale. The dataset contains 150K unique assembly steps, totaling over 900K multimodal samples. To enhance both visual and linguistic robustness, we augment each assembly step with diverse renderings and instruction granularities. Specifically, each step is rendered in three styles—Freestyle, Non-Freestyle, and Lineart—where Freestyle produces visually realistic images aligned with practical manuals at the cost of higher rendering time, while Lineart offers a more efficient but less detailed alternative. In parallel, we provide two levels of textual instructions: precise instructions that describe each step explicitly (e.g., “attach the first footstool leg to the seat”) and vague instructions that follow a generic template (e.g., “Assemble the {category} object”), specifying only the object category. 2) Rich Diversity. While existing assembly datasets are limited to categories such as tables and chairs, AssemBench covers over 50 object categories spanning furniture, daily objects, and fragments, fostering broad assembly spatial understanding during SFT. 3) High Quality. We rigorously ensure data quality: 6D pose labels are generated through deterministic geometric computation, guaranteeing label precision; textual instructions are annotated via rejection sampling with multi-model cross-validation to select high-quality semantic descriptions, ensuring multimodal annotation consistency. 4) Easy Scalability. Our data generation pipeline seamlessly scales using diverse sources, including existing part-level datasets and extensive web-scale visual assets, enabling continuous expansion.

Data Generation. Fig. 3 illustrates our progressive data construction pipeline, which combines part-level dataset adaptation with generative expansion to enable general MMLLMs to perform assembly-centric spatial reasoning. 1) Part-Level Mesh Preparation. We curate a diverse collection of assembly parts by consolidating and standardizing existing part-level datasets, including PartNet [29], BiAssembly [36], TwoByTwo [33], PartNeXt [44], and IKEA-Manual [45], with unified formats and coordinate systems. As existing datasets alone provide limited category coverage, we further expand part assets using generative models, directly synthesizing part-level meshes via PartPacker [39] to substantially improve diversity. 2) Assembly Data Generation. Given a set of part meshes, we first infer a valid assembly sequence based on spatial coordinates and part connectivity. Then we employ Blender [11] to automatically generate step-by-step assembly manuals that visualize relative part poses at each stage, while simultaneously sampling point clouds for the parts involved in each step, yielding consistent visual and 3D representations. 3) Rejection Sampling-Based Semantic Annotation. To align visual assembly cues with natural language, we generate semantic descriptions for each part from its manuals and category attributes, and compose step-level assembly instructions by jointly considering part semantics and assembly manuals. To ensure annotation quality, multiple VLMs (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B) independently produce candidate instructions, and a stronger model (e.g., GPT-5.2 [37]) serves as a judge to select the optimal annotation, ensuring both correctness and linguistic diversity. Additional details on the data generation pipeline are provided in Appx. -B.

IV Experiments

In this section, we systematically evaluate the AssemLM model through the following research questions:

  • •

    How does AssemLM compare with state-of-the-art assembly-specific methods and multimodal foundation models on standard benchmarks, and can a single trained model robustly handle diverse assembly categories with cross-category generalization?

  • •

    Can AssemLM achieve strong performance on previously unseen dataset sources and novel assembly categories under a zero-shot evaluation setting?

  • •

    Is AssemLM’s prediction accuracy sufficient for real-world assembly tasks, and how well does it perform on high-precision, multi-step assembly tasks?

Additional Details. More baseline comparisons (Appx. -C4), ablation studies (Appx. -C3), modality analysis (Appx. -C6), and experimental details (Appx. -C1 and -C5) are provided in Appx. -C.

IV-A Benchmark Comparison on Multi-Category Assembly Tasks

To evaluate AssemLM’s capacity for unified geometric reasoning, we conduct a comprehensive benchmark comparison across diverse object categories, including daily objects, furniture, and fragments.

Data Split and Input Standardization. We conduct all experiments on AssemBench. The dataset is divided into training and testing sets with a 9:1 ratio, with the split performed jointly over object categories and asset sources so that each category-source combination is represented in both sets. For fair comparison across model architectures under the multimodal design of AssemLM, we standardize the inputs at each assembly step. Specifically, we use only the freestyle-rendered assembly manuals and the corresponding vague instruction, forming a curated training set of approximately 130K unique state–pose pairs. This setting avoids introducing additional visual or linguistic variants for the same assembly step. All input point clouds are fully S​O​(3)SO(3) randomized.

Experimental Setup and Baselines. Unlike category-specific methods, we train a single, unified AssemLM model on the aforementioned 130K training samples without per-category fine-tuning. We compare AssemLM against two distinct classes of baselines:  1) Specialized Assembly Models. We evaluate TwoByTwo [33], a state-of-the-art framework specifically designed for robotic assembly. It leverages S​E​(3)SE(3)-equivariant representations to achieve high-precision part mating.  2) General-Purpose Foundation Models. To assess the inherent reasoning ceiling of large-scale models, we include GPT-5.2 [37] and DeepSeek-V3.2 [25]. These foundation models are evaluated by leveraging their pre-trained spatial commonsense and chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities. Additional baselines are included in Appx. -C.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate assembly performance using three complementary metrics: 1) RMSE(T), which measures translation accuracy by computing the root mean squared error between predicted and ground-truth translations. 2) Symmetric Chamfer Distance (SCD), which is used instead of raw rotation error to account for rotational symmetries. It is defined as twice the Chamfer Distance (S​C​D=2×C​DSCD=2\times CD), capturing the bidirectional geometric discrepancy between assembled shapes. 3) Success Rate (SR), which denotes the proportion of successful trials, where an assembly is considered successful if S​C​D<0.02SCD<0.02 (i.e., C​D<0.01CD<0.01).

Results and Analysis. Table I summarizes the quantitative results across three broad object categories: Furniture, Fragments, and Daily Objects. AssemLM consistently outperforms all baselines, demonstrating strong performance on multi-category part assembly. Overall, AssemLM achieves an average Success Rate (SR) of 89.4%, substantially higher than TwoByTwo (14.5%). In terms of precision, AssemLM attains a mean RMSE(T) of 0.0203, which is an order of magnitude lower than competing methods. On high-precision tasks such as Nut, Key, and Spoon, it reaches near-perfect success rates (90%–100%), highlighting its ability to capture fine-grained geometric constraints required for exact part mating.

Beyond raw performance, the results reveal clear limitations of existing approaches. Methods based solely on geometric equivariance (e.g., TwoByTwo) struggle to generalize across diverse topologies, while large foundation models (e.g., GPT-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2) fail to produce numerically accurate poses despite access to structured 3D inputs, often yielding semantically plausible but spatially incorrect predictions. In contrast, AssemLM remains robust across all domains, achieving consistently high SRs (86.9%–91.5%) and substantially outperforming baselines on the most challenging fragment assemblies. These results demonstrate that grounding multimodal reasoning in explicit geometric representations is essential for precise and generalizable robotic assembly.

IV-B Zero-Shot Generalization to Unseen Datasets and Categories

To further evaluate the robustness and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of AssemLM, we conduct a zero-shot evaluation on the standard IKEA datasets [45]. Unlike the previous multi-category benchmark, these assets were strictly excluded from the training phase. This experiment aims to verify whether the diverse geometric reasoning learned from our 130K large-scale dataset, under heavy rotation randomization, can generalize to assemblies from unseen asset sources and object categories.

Experimental Setup. We utilize the same models configured as described in §IV-A. The test set comprises three representative furniture categories: Bench, Chair, and Desk, among which Bench and Desk are unseen categories during training.

Results and Discussion. The zero-shot results in Table II demonstrate that AssemLM generalizes effectively to unseen assembly distributions. While the performance of TwoByTwo drops sharply on IKEA datasets (6.5% SR), AssemLM maintains a high success rate of 81.0%, indicating that its multimodal training on 130K samples enables the learning of generalized geometric mating principles that are not tied to specific dataset sources. Despite full S​O​(3)SO(3) randomization of part orientations, AssemLM achieves an average RMSE(T) of 0.0263, suggesting strong robustness to rotational variation and effective decoupling of translation and rotation for complex furniture joints. In contrast, large foundation models such as GPT-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 perform poorly on IKEA assets, with success rates below 5%. This further validates that without specialized geometric grounding, pre-trained common sense alone cannot resolve the complex spatial configurations required for structural furniture assembly.

IV-C Real-World Experiments

To verify whether the model’s prediction accuracy is sufficient to meet the requirements of real-world manipulation tasks, we conduct evaluations using a Flexiv Rizon 4s robotic arm on four highly challenging tasks.

Task Design. As shown in Fig. 4, we construct four challenging real-world tasks—Insert Plug, Store Cans, Insert Flower, and Build Blocks—covering both high-precision and multi-step assembly scenarios. 1) Insert Plug. The robot must insert a plug 1.5 cm deep into a power strip, with an error tolerance below 0.1 cm, making this task highly sensitive to translational prediction accuracy. 2) Store Cans. The robot is required to sequentially place four cans into a basket, testing not only placement precision but also the model’s ability to reason over multiple steps and identify the correct target region from the assembly manual. 3) Insert Flower. The robot must precisely insert a 23.3 cm-tall flower with a curved stem into a vase, which particularly challenges rotational prediction accuracy. 4) Build Blocks. The robot must complete a two-step block assembly task, in which the stability of the first placement directly affects the outcome of the second, thus requiring accurate multi-step execution. Detailed task descriptions are provided in Appx. -C5, and step visualizations are shown in Fig. 7.

Experimental Setup. For every assembly step in all tasks, we construct the point clouds, manuals, and instructions as model inputs. Following the previous experiments, the manuals are rendered in the Freestyle style and the instructions adopt the vague format. Detailed construction procedures are provided in Appx. -A1, and visualizations are shown in Fig. 5 and Fig. 7.

Built upon the large-scale pretrained models in §IV-A, we further fine-tune AssemLM and TwoByTwo on datasets constructed from real-world assets. During training and evaluation, we apply randomized translational and rotational perturbations to better simulate realistic conditions. All models are evaluated under 30 randomized initializations with seeds 0–29, and we report the execution success rate of the predicted assembly actions. Additional implementation details are provided in Appx. -C5.

Results and Discussion. Table III reports the task success rates on four real-world assembly tasks. AssemLM consistently outperforms TwoByTwo across all tasks, indicating stronger robustness and better generalization to real-world assets. In particular, AssemLM achieves higher success on Insert Plug, a task requiring precise control of both translation and rotation, which suggests improved fine-grained pose reasoning under high-precision constraints. AssemLM also delivers better performance on multi-step tasks such as Store Cans and Build Blocks. Overall, it achieves an average success rate of 50.8%, compared with 24.0% for TwoByTwo.

Step-wise Analysis. To further analyze performance in multi-step execution, Table IV reports the step-wise success rates on the Store Cans task. Although the overall task success declines as errors accumulate over sequential steps, AssemLM consistently maintains high per-step success rates, exceeding 80% for individual placements. We attribute this strong performance to AssemLM’s effective multimodal fusion. Even when the assembly manuals are partially occluded, as shown in Fig. 7, the model can still extract task-critical cues and compensate for the sparse point cloud observations of the cans. In contrast, TwoByTwo often repeatedly places cans into the same slot, suggesting limited ability to reason about slot occupancy and evolving task state across steps. These results indicate that most failures arise from long-horizon error accumulation rather than inaccurate single-step pose prediction, further highlighting AssemLM’s robust step-level spatial reasoning in real-world settings.

V Conclusion

We presented AssemLM, a spatial multimodal large language model tailored for high-precision robotic assembly. Our framework effectively bridges the gap between semantic reasoning and geometric execution by integrating a DeepStack-enhanced vision encoder with an SE(3)-equivariant point cloud encoder. By performing multimodal fusion at the embedding level, we utilize M-ROPE positional indices to maintain consistent spatial alignment for visual tokens while seamlessly injecting 3D geometric features. Furthermore, we introduced a specialized assembly pose tokenizer that stabilizes 6D pose prediction through a discrete-vocabulary interface. Validated on AssemBench, our large-scale benchmark with over 900K samples, AssemLM achieves state-of-the-art performance and demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization on unseen simulated benchmarks and strong performance on real-world assembly tasks.

-A Implementation Details of AssemLM

-A1 Generalization to Real-World Assets

To evaluate the transferability of AssemLM, we extend our framework to physical objects by leveraging the unique characteristics of real-world data acquisition. Unlike web-scale images that are often restricted to a single viewpoint and holistic object-level context, real-world assets provide two distinct advantages for geometric reasoning. First, the ability to capture multi-view imagery facilitates a more comprehensive spatial understanding. Second, each constituent part can be independently associated with its own set of high-resolution images, allowing 3D generative models to produce high-fidelity, part-level meshes with intricate geometry and authentic textured appearances. This granular representation effectively bridges the domain gap between synthetic training and physical deployment.

As illustrated in Fig. 5, we employ the Hunyuan3D [50] model to generate high-fidelity 3D models for each part of the task-specific assets used in our experiments. Following the automated dataset construction pipeline described in Appx. -B, these real-world assets are further organized into a structured dataset format suitable for training AssemLM.

By integrating external pose estimation modules such as FoundationPose [46], it is possible to obtain accurate 6D pose information for each object in real-world environments. Moreover, when combined with grasp prediction methods (e.g., GraspNet [15] and AnyGrasp [14]) and low-level motion planners for robotic manipulators, our framework could potentially be extended into a complete real-world robotic assembly pipeline, spanning perception, reasoning, and execution.

More importantly, the assembly pose prediction capability exhibited by AssemLM suggests its potential applicability beyond end-to-end policy learning. In particular, it could serve as a high-level spatial reasoning module in non-end-to-end manipulation frameworks [20, 30], as well as in simulation data generation pipelines [8, 23], where determining where to place an object remains a central challenge.

-A2 Special Tokens and Chat Template Design

As shown in Fig. 2, to equip the language model backbone with the ability to process multimodal inputs, we extend Qwen3-VL by introducing special tokens specifically designed for point cloud information. In particular, the token <PC_START> is used to indicate the beginning of point cloud input, <PC_END> denotes its termination, and additional tokens are employed to encode structured geometric features.

-A3 Model Architecture Details

Following Qwen3-VL-2B, our vision encoder adopts the SigLIP-2 architecture, specifically SigLIP2-Large (300M). It comprises a patch embedding layer, positional encoding modules, and 24 stacked vision transformer blocks, with a hidden size of 1024, an MLP intermediate dimension of 4096, and 16 attention heads. We further extract intermediate visual features from vision blocks 5, 11, and 17, process them with three DeepStack merger modules (each consisting of a LayerNorm and a two-layer MLP), and inject them into the first three transformer layers of the large language model backbone.

For the point cloud encoder, Vector Neuron DGCNN produces both an SE(3)-equivariant feature FF and an SE(3)-invariant feature GG, each of dimension (1024,3)(1024,3). Accordingly, the feature hyperparameter ff introduced in Sec. III-B is set to 1024. After the modality projectors, the two manual images and the two part point clouds are embedded into representations of size (648,2048)(648,2048) and (512,2048)(512,2048), respectively, before being injected into the transformer backbone.

-B AssemBench Dataset and Production Pipeline

As mentioned in Sec. III-C, we generate a precise and logically ordered assembly sequence for each asset to ensure geometric validity and correct part connectivity throughout the assembly process. To satisfy the training requirements described in Sec. III-A, we further construct multimodal supervision for each assembly step in the sequence, including high-fidelity point clouds, structured assembly manuals, and corresponding textual instructions (see Fig. 11). In the following, we describe the dataset in detail, organized according to the data generation procedure.

-B1 Asset Normalization and Canonical Coordinate System

To standardize all assets for downstream processing and model inference, we define a canonical coordinate system that unifies object scale and spatial placement, as illustrated in Fig. 6. Specifically, we first rotate each asset into a consistent z-up orientation. For example, assets from the IKEA-Manual [45] are originally defined in a y-up coordinate system and are therefore rotated accordingly. We then normalize the object scale by rescaling the longest axis to unit length, translate the object such that its center is aligned with the origin in the horizontal plane, and place the lowest point of the object at zero height along the vertical axis. This normalization procedure yields a physically plausible configuration that mimics objects resting on the ground in real-world scenes, while providing a unified geometric representation for learning and reasoning.

-B2 Point Cloud Sampling and Assembly Order Verification

After transforming all assets into the canonical coordinate system, we perform surface point cloud sampling for each part. Specifically, we first apply area-weighted surface sampling using the trimesh library to randomly sample 10,240 surface points per part, and then employ Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) to downsample them to 1,024 points. Compared to using area-weighted sampling alone, this two-stage strategy yields a more uniformly distributed and geometrically representative point cloud, preserving critical local structures such as sharp edges and fine connectors that are essential for accurate assembly reasoning and downstream 6D pose estimation.

Using the sampled point clouds of each part, we construct a binary connectivity matrix MM, where Mi​jM_{ij} indicates whether parts oio_{i} and ojo_{j} are physically connected. The part oo definition follows Sec. III-A. Specifically, two parts oio_{i} and ojo_{j} are considered connected if the minimum Euclidean Distance between their corresponding surface point clouds PiP_{i} and PjP_{j} is below a predefined threshold τ\tau, i.e.,

Mi​j=𝕀⁡(minp∈Pi,q∈Pj⁡∥p−q∥2<τ),τ=0.06.M_{ij}=\mathbb{I}\!\left(\min_{p\in P_{i},\;q\in P_{j}}\lVert p-q\rVert_{2}<\tau\right),\quad\tau=0.06. (4)

We maintain two dynamic part sets: an assembled set 𝒪a\mathcal{O}^{a} and an unassembled set 𝒪u\mathcal{O}^{u}. Given an assembly consisting of nn parts with an ordering {o0,…,on−1}\{o_{0},\dots,o_{n-1}\}, each assembly step sis_{i} is abstracted as selecting a part oio_{i} from 𝒪iu\mathcal{O}^{u}_{i} and moving it into 𝒪ia\mathcal{O}^{a}_{i}, yielding updated sets 𝒪i+1a\mathcal{O}^{a}_{i+1} and 𝒪i+1u\mathcal{O}^{u}_{i+1}. This process iterates until all parts are assembled.

At the initial step (i=0i=0), we select the base part with the lowest vertical extent:

o0=arg⁡mino∈𝒪0u​minp∈Po​pz,o_{0}=\arg\min_{o\in\mathcal{O}^{u}_{0}}\;\min_{p\in P_{o}}\;p_{z}, (5)

where pzp_{z} denotes the zz-coordinate of point pp.

For subsequent steps (i≥1i\geq 1), we restrict candidate parts to those connected to the current assembled set according to MM, and select the one with the lowest vertical extent:

oi=argmino∈Ciminp∈Popz,Ci={o∈𝒪iu|∃o′∈𝒪ia,Mo​o′=1}.o_{i}=\arg\min_{o\in C_{i}}\;\min_{p\in P_{o}}\;p_{z},C_{i}=\left\{o\in\mathcal{O}^{u}_{i}\;\middle|\;\exists\,o^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}^{a}_{i},\;M_{oo^{\prime}}=1\right\}. (6)

This strategy enforces part connectivity while assembling components in a bottom-up manner, thereby ensuring both structural validity and geometric feasibility throughout the assembly process.

Based on the determined assembly order and the sampled point clouds, we derive the fixed and moving point cloud representations for each assembly step, denoted as 𝒫ifixed\mathcal{P}^{\text{fixed}}_{i} and 𝒫imoving\mathcal{P}^{\text{moving}}_{i}, respectively, as defined in Sec. III-A. Specifically, the moving point cloud is given by

𝒫imoving=Pi,\mathcal{P}^{\text{moving}}_{i}=P_{i}, (7)

while the fixed point cloud aggregates all previously assembled parts. To maintain a consistent point cloud resolution across steps, we further apply FPS to downsample the union of fixed parts to 1024 points:

𝒫ifixed=FPS⁡(P0∪⋯∪Pi−1).\mathcal{P}^{\text{fixed}}_{i}=\mathrm{FPS}\!\left(P_{0}\cup\cdots\cup P_{i-1}\right). (8)

-B3 Instruction Manual Generation

For each assembly step sis_{i}, we provide a pair of rendered images before and after the assembly, denoted as IibeforeI_{i}^{\text{before}} and IiafterI_{i}^{\text{after}}, which serve as visual instruction manuals to guide the model in understanding the intended assembly operation. These images provide step-specific spatial cues that complement the geometric information from point clouds, enabling the model to infer the correct 6D assembly pose. Such visual guidance is particularly important for tasks with multiple valid attachment locations, e.g., selecting the correct mounting position for one of several identical furniture legs, or determining the appropriate placement slot in real-world storage tasks such as arranging cans in a basket.

To generate the instruction manuals, we sequentially insert the normalized assets {o0,…,on−1}\{o_{0},\dots,o_{n-1}\} into a Blender [11] scene following the determined assembly order. This process produces a sequence of rendered images {I0,…,In−1}\{I_{0},\dots,I_{n-1}\}, where for assembly step sis_{i}, the pre- and post-assembly images are defined as Iibefore=IiI_{i}^{\text{before}}=I_{i} and Iiafter=Ii+1I_{i}^{\text{after}}=I_{i+1}, satisfying Iiafter=Ii+1beforeI_{i}^{\text{after}}=I_{i+1}^{\text{before}}. This formulation ensures temporal consistency between consecutive assembly steps.

To enrich the visual diversity of the dataset, we render each assembly step using three complementary rendering styles: Freestyle, Non-Freestyle, and Lineart (see Fig. 10). The Freestyle style performs a topology-aware edge detection after photorealistic rendering, producing line drawings with fine structural details that highlight critical assembly features. While highly informative, this mode incurs a higher rendering cost, with an average rendering time of 8.59 seconds per image, depending on scene complexity and Cycles sampling settings. The Non-Freestyle style disables edge extraction and yields standard pixel-based renderings, offering faster rendering at an average of 3.35 seconds per image, albeit with less explicit structural emphasis. The Lineart style leverages Blender’s Grease Pencil system and its Line Art modifier to algorithmically extract feature lines directly in 3D space and project them into vectorized 2D drawings. This approach achieves significantly faster rendering (0.22 seconds per image on average), though the resulting visuals are coarser and may contain noise. Together, these complementary rendering styles balance visual fidelity, structural clarity, and computational efficiency, providing diverse and informative supervision for multimodal assembly reasoning.

-C Experimental Details and Supplementary Experiments

-C1 Implementation Details

For the benchmark comparison experiments in §IV-A, the zero-shot generalization experiments in §IV-B, as well as the supplementary baseline comparisons in Appx. -C4 and ablation studies in Appx. -C3, all trainable models are trained on the same 130K training samples for 12 epochs under identical settings. Specifically, we adopt the same hyperparameters (e.g., per_gpu_batch_size=4 and temperature=1) and the same training environment consisting of 4×\timesA100/H100 GPUs, each with 80GB memory. For the foundation models, we serialize sampled point coordinates into structured text tokens to facilitate spatial reasoning. Concretely, for each part, we sample 1024 points and represent them as comma-separated 3D coordinate tuples in the form of (x,y,z)(x,y,z). These coordinates are combined with the before/after assembly manuals and the task instruction to form the multimodal prompt, and the model is required to predict the 9D pose vector in list form, parameterized by 3D translation and a 6D continuous rotation representation. All input point clouds are normalized and augmented with random S​O​(3)SO(3) rotations. Moreover, the same set of randomized initial poses is used across all evaluations to ensure a fair and consistent comparison.

-C2 Additional Experimental Setup

As shown in Tables VI and V, DO, Fur., Frag., and R-T denote Daily Objects, Furniture, Fragments, and RMSE(T), respectively, following the same conventions as in §IV-A and §IV-B. To further validate the advantages of AssemLM, we introduce two additional experimental settings. First, compared with §IV-B, we extend Fur.* to the full IKEA datasets [45] by additionally including the shelf, table, and misc categories, where misc consists of a mixture of uncategorized furniture items. This setting poses a more challenging test of the model’s reasoning ability on unseen categories and assets from unseen sources. Second, to better assess rotational prediction, we introduce the metric SCD(R), which measures the Chamfer Distance induced solely by rotational error under accurate translation. We do not adopt Geodesic Distance or RMSE(R) because many assembly parts are symmetric, such that multiple rotations can be equally valid, and these metrics may therefore over-penalize correct predictions.

-C3 Ablation Studies

To validate the contributions of different input modalities and architectural components, we conduct both modality and module ablations.

For modality ablation, we train and evaluate the model with one modality removed at a time, and report the results in the top part of Table V. Removing vision or point cloud input leads to substantial degradation in translation and rotation accuracy, respectively, while removing text causes a moderate drop in both. These results highlight the importance of jointly leveraging multiple modalities for accurate assembly pose prediction.

For module ablation, the results in the bottom part of Table V show that removing each key design component leads to performance degradation to different extents. This confirms that each module contributes positively to the overall performance of AssemLM.

-C4 Additional Comparative Experiments

We additionally include ManualPA [49], which predicts assembly actions from manuals and point clouds, and SE(3)-Assembly [47], which predicts assembly poses using SE(3)-equivariant representations, as supplementary baselines. As shown in Table VI, our method achieves higher prediction accuracy than both baselines, with particularly notable gains in translation estimation, where it substantially outperforms ManualPA.

-C5 Additional Details of Real-World Experiments

For the real-world experiments in §IV-C, we design four challenging tasks that cover both fine-grained manipulation and multi-step assembly to validate the effectiveness of our model. The four tasks—Insert Plug, Store Cans, Insert Flower, and Build Blocks—are described in detail below:

  • •

    Insert Plug. The robot is required to insert a charger plug into a standard power strip to initiate phone charging. Unlike prior works that introduce adapters or enlarged sockets to increase tolerance [33], we directly use a real charger plug with metal contacts of size 0.6​cm×0.1​cm,0.6\,\text{cm}\times 0.1\,\text{cm,} and a standard socket opening of 0.8​cm×0.2​cm0.8\,\text{cm}\times 0.2\,\text{cm}. Successful execution requires controlling the lateral alignment error within 0.1​cm0.1\,\text{cm} and fully inserting the 1.5​cm1.5\,\text{cm}-deep plug. This task places extremely strict demands on the model’s 6D pose prediction accuracy in both translation and rotation.

  • •

    Store Cans. This task evaluates multi-step reasoning and execution accuracy. The robot sequentially places four identical cans into distinct compartments of a plastic basket. A single failure in any step causes the entire task to fail. Each can has a circular base of 7​cm7\,\text{cm} diameter, while each target compartment is a 7.5​cm×7.5​cm7.5\,\text{cm}\times 7.5\,\text{cm} square, leaving minimal clearance. Moreover, due to the large spatial extent of the basket, point cloud sampling under a fixed budget (1024 points) yields sparse observations of the cans within the 𝒫fixed\mathcal{P}^{\text{fixed}} representation. Since all 𝒫moving\mathcal{P}^{\text{moving}} are geometrically similar, the model must rely on subtle geometric differences in sparse point clouds to infer slot occupancy and reason about the valid target slot for the current step.

  • •

    Insert Flower. In this task, the robot inserts a flower into a vase while maintaining the vase’s stability (see Fig. 5). We select flowers with significant stem curvature: although bent, the flower height reaches 45​cm45\,\text{cm}, nearly twice the vase height of 23.2​cm23.2\,\text{cm}. The horizontal projection of the curved stem spans approximately 20​cm20\,\text{cm}, while the vase opening diameter is only 6​cm6\,\text{cm}. Accurate rotation prediction is therefore critical; even small orientation errors can cause lateral displacement of the stem, resulting in collision and tipping of the vase.

  • •

    Build Blocks. This task requires assembling a block-based chair in two sequential steps. First, the robot inserts the seat component onto four vertical legs simultaneously. Each peg has a diameter of only 0.5​cm0.5\,\text{cm}, and all four contact points must align precisely; otherwise, early contact induces lateral forces that displace the remaining legs, leading to failure. The second step inserts the backrest onto the assembled seat, where any residual error from the first step accumulates and further amplifies task difficulty. This task strongly challenges both translational and rotational precision as well as error accumulation across steps.

During fine-tuning and evaluation of AssemLM and TwoByTwo on datasets constructed from real-world assets, we apply translational perturbations within a range of 0.1 on the horizontal plane in the canonical coordinate system, together with rotational perturbations of up to 10∘, to simulate randomized initial conditions. All models are fine-tuned for 330 epochs with a batch size of 4 and evaluated under 30 randomized initializations with seeds 0–29. In experiments, the grasp poses are predefined, while the assembly poses are predicted by the model, ensuring that the comparison results directly reflect each model’s assembly pose prediction capability.

-C6 Modality Contribution Analysis

To further investigate the influence of different modalities on the reasoning process of AssemLM, we conduct an interpretability analysis of its attention mechanisms. Specifically, we extract the cross-attention weights from the final transformer layer during inference and average them over the test set to quantify how much the model attends to each input modality when predicting the assembly pose tokens.

As illustrated in Fig. 8 (Right), the model exhibits a strong dependency on 3D geometric representations. The SE(3)-equivariant features of the fixed part (PC1) and the correlation features of the moving part (PC2) collectively account for 82.0% of the total attention weight (56.6% and 25.4%, respectively). This overwhelming dominance confirms that AssemLM correctly grounds its assembly reasoning in precise S​E​(3)SE(3) spatial data rather than relying on superficial visual or linguistic priors. The high attention on PC1 suggests that the model prioritizes understanding the geometry of the target placement site, i.e., the fixed part, to anchor its predictions.

While geometry remains central to precise pose estimation, visual and linguistic inputs provide essential context. 2D schematic images account for approximately 14.3% of the model’s attention (Image 1: 6.0%, Image 2: 8.3%), suggesting that rendered manuals help infer global structural context and resolve part-identity ambiguities that pure point clouds may lack. In contrast, text instructions contribute only 3.8%. This distribution aligns with the requirements of pose regression: while language clarifies the task intent, it lacks the high-frequency spatial precision necessary for geometric alignment.

-C7 Further Analysis on Data and Design Choices

To further investigate the factors affecting AssemLM’s performance, we conduct a set of additional analyses on the impact of dataset scale, rotation randomization range, and tokenizer design on geometric reasoning. We consider four experimental settings to examine these factors in a controlled manner, as detailed below:

  • •

    AssemLM (Full). The proposed model trained on the full curated dataset of 130K samples with full S​O​(3)SO(3) rotation randomization.

  • •

    AssemLM (350-S). A low-data variant trained exclusively on the 350 samples from the daily object subset of the TwoByTwo dataset, designed to evaluate data efficiency.

  • •

    AssemLM (Lim-Rot). A constrained variant where the rotation randomization is restricted to ±45∘\pm 45^{\circ} during both training and testing, assessing the model’s sensitivity to pose distribution.

  • •

    AssemLM (Fast-Tk). A variant utilizing the FastTokenizer architecture instead of our custom pose tokenizer, aimed at evaluating the effectiveness of our discretization strategy.

As illustrated in Fig. 9, quantitative results indicate that the scale of the training data is the most decisive factor for generalization. AssemLM (350-S), limited to only 350 samples, fails to capture the underlying geometric manifolds, resulting in a high average RMSE(T) of 0.0475. In contrast, AssemLM (Full) leverages the 130K samples to achieve a significantly lower error of 0.0317, demonstrating that large-scale multimodal pre-training is essential for learning universal assembly priors. Regarding rotation randomization, while AssemLM (Lim-Rot) achieves localized precision in constrained settings, it offers no significant advantage over the Full model, suggesting that full rotation training does not compromise local accuracy while enabling broader generalization.

Furthermore, the comparison between AssemLM (Full) and AssemLM (Fast-Tk) highlights the importance of the tokenizer design. We observe a distinct performance degradation in the FastTokenizer variant, with RMSE(T) increasing to 0.0366. This suggests that generic subword tokenizers are ill-suited for geometric regression due to the resulting variable-length sequences—often exceeding 9 tokens—and the increased autoregressive burden. Unlike our training-free, uniform discretization strategy, the FastTokenizer incurs additional training overhead and redundancy without offering accuracy gains, confirming that our custom tokenizer provides a more stable and effective interface for geometric grounding.

-D Qualitative Visualizations and Dataset Examples

To provide a more intuitive understanding of AssemLM’s reasoning process and the richness of our training data, we present qualitative visualizations of both the dataset assets and the model’s predictive performance.

As shown in Fig. 10 and Fig. 11, AssemBench provides high-fidelity multimodal supervision, covering a vast array of geometric structures and artistic rendering styles for instruction manuals. This diversity is key to the model’s robust cross-modal alignment.

Furthermore, Fig. 12 demonstrates AssemLM’s predictive accuracy on unseen test assets. The high degree of overlap between the predicted poses and the ground-truth configurations highlights the model’s ability to resolve fine-grained spatial constraints. Even when faced with ambiguous manual instructions or sparse point clouds, the model generates physically plausible and precise assembly anchors, confirming the effectiveness of our pose discretization and multimodal fusion strategy.
